questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The study environment was important to me - both on an academic and social level.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I could take so many experiences with me home. New knowledge, friendships, insights, and experiences.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Through the ESN organisation and their introduction events, I was made aware of registering for a BSN in the Netherlands and which banks could be a good idea to contact if I wanted to open a Dutch bank account (I used ING and was very satisfied with it). However, it was still difficult to figure out all the necessary steps upon arrival as there was quite a lot to register in the beginning.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The people behind the ESN organization were very helpful with answering questions, but I did feel a lot on my own with a lot of stuff. However, it was always possible to contact the host university and ask questions.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: They did help through e-mail, but it was a slow process. I couldn't find any phone numbers to call - that I was very unsatisfied with.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I signed up to get a housing offer through the host institution and was very lucky with the dorm I found. I strongly recommend you to sign up as well and check your mail as often as you can afterward. Because as soon as they send you an offer, you have to be fast. Luckily, I was and I applied for a room at the dorm located at Prinsengracht - one of the most beautiful areas in Amsterdam. I spoke with many other students who hadn't been fast enough and therefore had to accept a room quite far from the center or not getting a room at all.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I had classes at three different faculties during my stay, so in the end (for me) it didn't matter that I didn't get to live close to one specific campus, as they were spread out over the city and it was easy for me to walk. (It would take 8, 20 or 45 minutes to walk depending on the location of the faculty). Even if you do not manage to find a room within the City Center of Amsterdam, do not worry. It is easy to rent a bike and you will get fast around the city.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As I wrote earlier, I was very fast and was one of the first people to book a room through the host institution after they send the invitation. You can choose the room and dorm you want, but only if they have not been taken by a student faster than you. Therefore, I was very, very satisfied with the housing available. However, I did meet many people who didn't get a room because there weren't fast enough.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Difficult. As I study communication and it, there were a lot of interesting communication-related courses I wanted, however, they were not part of the courses they offered at the Faculty of Humanities. Instead, the communication subjects were offered through another faculty, but I could only apply for two subjects outside of the Faculty of Humanities. That was a real shame, and I had to take some classes that weren't relevant to me.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I do not remember the registration process that well. But it was a intuitive process when signing up for classes at the Faculty of Humanities - more difficult to sign up at another faculty, but I did contact my host university through mail to get the help I needed.

They have a block system, so you'll have to figure out how you want to spread the different classes between the 2-3 blocks. I took 3 subjects during the first block, 1 during the second block, and 1 during the third block. Three classes in one block is harder but manageable.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I did contact my host university and they helped me. However, there was no number I could call, so all contact happened through e-mail which was slow and a bit frustrating.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I only got 2 subjects I really wanted (out of 5). One subject was very popular and I wasn't fast enough to register. The other two subjects I wanted were at another faculty, and unfortunately, I couldn't apply for more than two, even though those subjects were the most relevant to me.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Check in advance which subjects you want and whether they are offered through the faculty that you'll go to or if there are offered through another faculty. And be fast when you have to register for courses - some of them get full very quickly.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Even though I took some classes that didn't interest me, the professors were very good and made the subject interesting.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I was intimidated by their grade scale: 1-10, as I had to have a grade above 5.5 to pass the subjects which seemed high to me. But if you read all texts, go to the lectures, and study for the exam, you will be fine.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
They were very familiar with each other. There were more hybrid teaching (zoom meetings and physical lectures), but that was mostly as a result of Corona. The teachers were very great and competent.
I think the academic level was similar to DK, but I was unfamiliar with the multiple-choice exam that they use quite a lot. But again, if you do your readings, you will be fine.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
(1) Topic The Role of Emotions in Political Communication
(2) Topic Health Communication: From Theory to Practice
(3) Making Media: Production, Practices, and Profession
(4) Media, Culture, and Sport
(5) The Five Senses of Cinema

1 = most interesting
5 = least interesting

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: "Topic The Role of Emotions in Political Communication" was my favorite course. It used many different contexts (e.g. the pandemic) as a way to affect people's emotions by framing messages in a specific way regarding political communication. Very interesting.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I got a bill after having contacted the hospital over the phone regarding an injury. However, as I am European citizen I did have my European Health Insurance card which meant, that I didn't have to pay but instead send documentation of this.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I think the transportation was a bit expensive, but mostly all prices were similar to Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The ESN organisation did a great job offering and creating social activities for the exchange students.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: ESN organized so many activities: parties, sports events, park chillout, bowling, Galla, dinner, etc. There was for sure something for everyone, which I really appreciated.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I got a mail asking if I wanted to sign up for "a local buddy" and I almost declined as I didn't know what it meant. However, I did say yes - because why not? And I'm glad I did. My local buddy ended up being a nice guy from the Netherlands who also studied at UvA and I became part of his group where I met other international students who ended up being some of my best friends at my exchange. With a "Buddy Group" you can ask your local buddy whatever questions you might have and during the stay and a few events will be created for the group to meet up and bond.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: To the beach, Zandvoort. Utrecht. Haarlem. The tulip fields or Keukenhof (if in season).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: As Amsterdam is a very intercultural city and familiar to DK, there were no big adjustments.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: The local students I socialized with were mainly through events organized by the ESN, so I'd recommend go to the events that interest you.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The Dutch people believe that their biking culture and infrastructure are better than ours in Denmark, which made it challenging not to start a discussion.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Every Saturday many neighborhoods in Amsterdam host large street markets, where local vendors gather together and sell goods ranging from organic produce grown in the Netherlands to second-hand clothing, antiques, and souvenirs. That part I really appreciated about their culture.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Everyone living in the Netherlands must have a citizen service number, often referred to as a BSN (burgerservicenummer) and you'll need to apply for that quite fast (and deregister when you leave).
2. Everyone is very nice - make sure to take a chance, sign up for the events, and meet people - especially in the beginning before everyone has found their own "group of people".
3. Sign up for a local buddy

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The healthcare system in the Netherlands is a bit difficult to figure out on your own if you need to see a doctor. In case you do need to see a doctor, you should go to the nearest General Practitioners (GP) from where you live. Normally, people register with a "huisarts" when they arrive in the Netherlands. I didn't do it and I don't know any exchange students who did, but it might be a good idea to make some research just so you'll know where to go, in case you need to see a doctor. You can always knock on their door and say that you live nearby and ask if you should register - I did when I got an injury. They told me, that I didn't need any medical help and that I didn't have to register as I had only 2 months left. However, they did tell me to come back if something else should happen to me, which was nice to know.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The social experiences and the friends I made. It always seem a bit more "dangourous" when it's hard to anticipate how the exchange will be, but as soon as you have arrived it is not that difficult to figure it all out and you'll meet a lot of great people.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Mostly the practical things: to register, get different kinds of approval, and constantly be in contact with my home and host university to figure out formalities.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Exchange is different for everyone. For me, I didn't feel lonely at any point. It all felt natural and I appreciated every second of it.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
